Meet Stargazer, a One-Off Tiny House With a Drop-Down Deck, Japanese Soaking Tub, and Murphy Bed
24 photos
Photo: Exploring Alternatives/YouTube screenshot
Many people keep clear of tiny living because they believe it implies serious trade-offs in regard to space and comfort. But what if a tiny house could offer the comfort of a conventional home, the mobility of an RV, and a slew of surprise features that maximize the use of space?
The Stargazer tiny house tries to make small-space living as comfortable and appealing as possible with multifunctional, convertible furniture, an expanding bathroom, and a rear wall that drops down to create an outdoor deck.
This clever tiny home on wheels is a one-off creation that was built as part of an experiment called The Tiny House Master Plan. The idea was to build a house completely for free, document the entire process as a show at no cost, and then give the finished home away to a lucky winner. The mastermind behind this project is Kenton Zerbin, a British Columbia-based sustainable living educator who lives in an off-grid tiny house of his own.
He aimed to create a home that was a peak example of good design, to demonstrate what can be achieved in a compact space with creativity, innovative ideas, and craftsmanship. He completed the project with help from over fifty sponsors, many volunteers, and students, all passionate about sustainable living, tiny homes , and community.
“What started as a bold experiment to build and give away a tiny house for free turned into one of the most challenging and meaningful projects I’ve ever taken on,” Kenton says.
Photo: Exploring Alternatives/YouTube screenshot In the video attached below, he explains that function took priority over appearance when designing the Stargazer. The result is a home that is not only livable but also highly efficient and ready to be used off-grid. Its base is a triple-axle gooseneck trailer from Timber Suspension Systems with a suspension system and built-in jacks on all four corners.
It measures 26 feet (7.9 meters) long at the base, with an extra 7 feet (2.1 meters) extending over the gooseneck section, bringing the total length to 33 feet (10 meters). With a width of 8.5 feet (2.6 meters), it can legally be transported on public roads without special permits.
Because it was built with the assumption that it would serve as a roving home , they designed it with lightweight materials and an aerodynamic shape. It features metal framing and aluminum siding to keep weight down, while the angled roof at the front lets air flow around it. The exterior is clad in a combination of black and natural wood-tone aluminum plank siding from FastPlank Systems, a diamond plate protects the front side, and storage compartments are integrated on both sides to hold utility equipment and other things you don’t want inside the house.
Photo: Exploring Alternatives/YouTube screenshot It’s also worth mentioning that Stargazer is designed for year-round living , with spray foam insulation all around, including underneath the trailer. It is also equipped with a heat recovery ventilation (HRV) system, which brings fresh air inside and exhausts stale air without losing heat.
Stargazer’s interior comes to roughly 280 square feet (26 square meters) and boasts a layout that puts the living area at the front, the kitchen in the middle, and the bathroom and bedroom toward the rear. What makes it highly functional is a series of innovative features that you don’t see in other tiny homes , such as an expanding bathroom with a Japanese-inspired soaker tub, a built-in deck that creates an open-air bedroom or home office, as well as transforming furniture like a Murphy bed and a convertible dinette.
The living area consists of two sofa benches and a cherrywood table operated by an electric lifting mechanism. When in raised position, the table creates a dining space for at least six people, and if you lower it and combine it with cushions, you get a large king-size bed. The whole front wall is full of storage cabinets; some hold the propane tanks and the rest are perfect for storing cushions, bedding, pillows, and more. A TV is mounted on the wall for entertainment.
Photo: Exploring Alternatives/YouTube screenshot The kitchen features long concrete countertops and incorporates a central peninsula that doubles as a bar, while the section next to the living room can serve as a desk. It functions just like a conventional kitchen in a “real” home thanks to a double-basin sink, a Dometic two-burner gas cooktop, a range hood, and an apartment-size refrigerator.
Cabinets surround the work area with much-needed storage, and large windows bring natural light inside. Kenton also added a small wood stove above the peninsula, adding both warmth and character.
A hallway leads to the private areas. Hallways are usually dead spaces in tiny homes, but Kenton didn’t want to waste any space, which is why he created a clever door system that allows the passage to become part of the bathroom. The doors basically close off the hallway, increasing the bathroom space by almost 33%.
Photo: Exploring Alternatives/YouTube screenshot The bathroom itself is fully tiled and includes a large shower stall with a cedar shower pan that lifts to reveal a Japanese soaker tub built into the floor. It’s made of lightweight concrete and offers a nice bathing experience. A compact vanity with a wall-mounted faucet and a Separett composting toilet are also included.
The bedroom at the rear is designed as a flexible space with a Murphy bed that gets out of the way when not needed and a large storage unit with cabinets. Owners can add a pivoting or flip-up desk to turn the room into a home office. One of the most surprising features, however, is the back wall, which drops down to form a built-in deck, extending the room to the outside.
The newly created opening comes with two screens - one serves as a projector screen for outdoor movie nights, while the other is a bug screen. The overhang above the deck acts as a natural awning.
Photo: Exploring Alternatives/YouTube screenshot As mentioned, the Stargazer was designed as a self-contained home , and its off-grid equipment includes solar panels, a charge controller, batteries, onboard water tanks, a composting toilet, and a small wood stove. Conventional RV hookups are also available, so the house can connect to the grid as well.
This one-of-a-kind tiny home was won by a family of four living on a farm, and they say it’s a great addition to their property.
The Stargazer project was intended to cost nothing through sponsorships and volunteer contributions, but a house like this still requires a great amount of resources. Kenton says he didn’t keep track of the team’s labor hours, but he estimates that materials alone cost between CAD $80,000 and $100,000 (USD $56,300 to $70,400), and that a professional builder would aks at least CAD $200,000 (USD $140,800) for a similar build.
